status: Provisional: drawn from other streaming projects' published claims, which each measure differently. Open to discussion.

bad_pictures.label: decode errors
bad_pictures.what: Frames the client failed to decode, or decoded corrupt, on every stream.
bad_pictures.basis: Decode failures plus corrupt decodes. Any is a bug: 100 with none, else 0.

missing_clean.label: lost frames
missing_clean.what: Frames that never reached the client's decoder on streams with nothing dropped.
missing_clean.basis: Frames that never arrived on streams with nothing dropped: 100 with none, 50 with up to 3.

frame_time_p99.label: frame pacing p99
frame_time_p99.what: The 99th percentile of the time between frames arriving at the client on clean streams, in frame intervals: 1 is perfect pacing.
frame_time_p99.basis: Gap between frame arrivals; one frame interval is perfect pacing. Rubylight reports 1.25 intervals on wired LAN, and loopback has no network to excuse more.

references.claim: arrival interval p99 20.9 ms, HEVC 1080p60, wired LAN, moonlight-common-c client

fps_delivered.label: delivered frame rate
fps_delivered.what: Frames the client received per second on clean streams, as a share of the stream's frame rate.
fps_delivered.basis: A host that can't keep up sends fewer, evenly spaced frames, which frame time alone misses.

server_p99_ms.label: host latency p99
server_p99_ms.what: The 99th percentile of Moonshine's time on the host from capturing a frame to sending its last packet.
server_p99_ms.basis: Mostly the encode, which scales with resolution, not frame rate. Other hosts report 0.45–4.4 ms.

references.claim: encode 2.6–3.1 ms at 1440p120 idle; mean host processing 0.45 ms on wired LAN
p50 ~0.8 ms capture → received at 720p120 on its punktfunk/1 protocol, NVIDIA zero-copy NVENC (README June–September 2026; span ends at the client, so it includes the network; machines not stated)
PyroWave encode p99 6.4 → 4.4 ms on an RTX 5070 Ti under GRID 2
4–8 ms end to end at 4K120 HDR on an RTX 4090 with encoding in the display driver, against 9–17 ms in-process (span not stated)

freeze_p95.label: recovery time p95
freeze_p95.what: The 95th percentile of how long the picture stood still after a lost frame, until a frame recovered it, in frame intervals.
freeze_p95.basis: How long the picture stands still after a loss. Recovery takes a round trip and an encode, so about three frame intervals is the floor; a keyframe takes longer.

references.claim: mean gap after a keyframe cut from 8.44 to 5.30 ms (HEVC, recovery cadence work)

recovered_without_keyframe.label: RFI recovery rate
recovered_without_keyframe.what: The share of lost frames the stream recovered from with reference frame invalidation (RFI) instead of a keyframe.
recovered_without_keyframe.basis: Losses recovered by reference frame invalidation, without a keyframe, which should make keyframes after a loss rare. Rubylight recovers 59 of 59 without one.

references.claim: AV1, 20 ms of video dropped every 1.5 s for 90 s: 59 of 59 lost frames recovered without a keyframe

click_median.label: input latency p50
click_median.what: The median time from the client sending a click to it decoding the flash the click caused (to decoded, not to photons), in frame intervals.
click_median.basis: From the injected click to the decoded flash. The app's next frame and its render take about one interval, so 1 is the floor.

references.claim: 5.89 ms median capture to client present, AV1 1080p60, loopback
7 ms median picture age, capture to rendered, Retroid Pocket 6 over Wi-Fi, HEVC 1080p60

keyframes_per_switch.label: HDR switch keyframes
keyframes_per_switch.what: Keyframes Moonshine sent per change in the captured content's color space (SDR, HDR10, scRGB).
keyframes_per_switch.basis: SDR ↔ HDR changes the color description, which takes a keyframe; HDR10 ↔ scRGB needn't. hdrneon's cycle puts the floor at 0.67.

load_fps.label: FPS under GPU load
load_fps.what: Frames the client received per second while the GPU was under heavy load, as a share of the stream's frame rate.
load_fps.basis: The slowest codec's frame rate with the GPU busy. Other hosts report 85–100% under load, and as low as 42% before fixes.

references.claim: 117–120 fresh pictures/s at 120 fps under GPU load; Vibepollo 2.0 103–118
a loaded NVIDIA host delivered about 25 of a game's 60 fps with 70 ms of encode latency, fixed by real-time GPU priority

peak_bitrate.label: peak bitrate
peak_bitrate.what: The busiest one-second window of bits the client received, as a share of the bitrate the stream asked for.
peak_bitrate.basis: Rate control should hold near the bitrate. Keyframes burst over it, and a link sized for the bitrate drops what doesn't fit.

unpublished.note: no published latency or pacing figures
no published latency or pacing figures
pacing features (adaptive packet pacing), no published figures

click_context.about: What a click's latency feels like next to everyday hardware. The test measures from the client injecting a click to the client finishing the decode of the flash, over loopback: no input device, network or display. The parts a real setup adds, and whole-chain measurements of local play and cloud streaming, come from published tests, each one setup and method; treat them as rough.

adds.label: wired mouse
adds.claim: RTINGS' example graph: one wired mouse's clicks at about 9–11 ms, its methodology counting under 10 ms as good

adds.label: Bluetooth mouse
adds.claim: RTINGS' example graph: the same mouse over Bluetooth at about 17–20 ms

adds.label: DualSense over Bluetooth
adds.claim: Gamepadla: 9.03 ms over Bluetooth (its comparison data is marked as in testing)

adds.label: OLED TV, game mode, 60 Hz
adds.claim: LG C3: 9.0 ms at 4K60 (Multiplayer.it, Leo Bodnar 4K lag tester) to 13.1 ms at 1080p60 (GamesRadar)
